name: Bianca Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a hill farm, so half my day is walking up something. We've got about ninety beef cows, Hereford crosses, hay meadows, and an old apple orchard that the owners press into juice and sell at the market. I check the cattle first thing, then it's whatever the season needs. Right now it's pruning the apple trees and feeding hay, because the grass has stopped. The cold in my hands by eleven is what wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who owns the farm, and who do you work with?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The Lindqvists, an older couple, and their son Erik who's taking over bit by bit. It's me, Erik and a part-timer called Yusuf. I've been there six years now, since I finished my certificate, and I know the place better than Erik does in some ways, though I'd never say that to him.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology or AI in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not really. There's a computer in the farm office for the cattle records, and Erik does that. I've got a phone that does calls and photos and that's all I want from it. My partner Marco laughs at me, and he's a mechanic at the tractor dealer, so he spends all day plugging laptops into engines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Most of the things people get excited about turn out to be about half as good as they said. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay as they are, and things are fine. Marco and I have been saving for a house for four years, and we've got enough for the deposit now. If nothing big changes, we'd just go ahead and buy, probably the cottage near the old mill if it's still for sale in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy the house in the spring, keep working at the Lindqvists'. Maybe ask Erik for a small rise, since he keeps saying I'm the one who holds it together. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, really, because it means we stop waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the house something you've been putting off because of things like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Marco keeps reading things about robots at the dealer, and every time he does, he says maybe we should wait one more year. If it all turned out to be hype, I could finally tell him to stop reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the rise be worth to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much in money, maybe the price of a new pair of boots a month. It's more that I'd like to hear it said. Six years is long enough to be treated as more than help.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because most exciting things turn out half as good as people said. I wouldn't post anything online, I don't really do that.
S0.think: It means things stay as they are, and things are fine. My partner and I have the deposit saved after four years, so we'd go ahead and buy the cottage by the old mill.
S0.do: Buys a house with her partner in the spring and keeps working at the same farm. Asks the farm's heir, Erik, for a small pay rise after six years.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, because it means they can stop waiting.
S0.quote: If it all turned out to be hype, I could finally tell him to stop reading.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca is matter-of-fact and slightly sceptical of anything new. Her main concern is the house purchase that her partner keeps delaying because of robot news. The pay rise is about respect as much as money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll take a long time to reach places like ours. You can't run a robot up a forty-degree slope in the rain and expect it to come back down in one piece. I'd say flat farms should worry first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm probably right about the hills, but I'm not sure about the rest. The hay and the feeding could get done by machines on the flat bits, and that's a good part of my work. I'd be less sure about the house, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and see what the flat farms do first. I wouldn't learn anything new unless Erik asked me to, and even then I'd want him to show me himself. We'd still buy the house, I think, but maybe a cheaper one so the mortgage is smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear the forecast and it might rain on the hay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a cheaper house. What would that mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not the mill cottage, but one of the terraced houses on Station Road. They're fine, they just don't have a garden. I'd miss the garden more than Marco would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn anything new unless asked. Why not get ahead of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched people get ahead of things that never happened. Erik's cousin spent a fortune on a milking robot and then sold the cows two years later. I'd rather be slow and not wrong.

S1.say: I'd say it'll take a long time to reach hill farms, because you can't run a robot up a steep slope in the rain. Flat farms should worry first.
S1.think: I'm probably right about the hills, but the hay and feeding on the flat bits could go to machines, and that's a good part of my work. I'd feel less sure about the house.
S1.do: Keeps working as before and watches what flat farms do first. Only learns new kit if the farm asks her to, and buys a cheaper house so the mortgage is smaller.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a forecast that might rain on the hay.
S1.quote: I'd rather be slow and not wrong.
S1.fieldNote: She uses the farm's steep land as a reason to feel safe, and half believes it. Her caution is backed by a real story about a neighbour's failed robot investment. The house plans shrink quietly, which tells more than her public line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see a robot pruning an apple tree properly. But I'd be scared too, and I'd probably say so to my mum and nobody else. In public I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's real, then two years is no time at all. I've got one skill, and it's this farm. The Lindqvists wouldn't keep me on if a robot did the cattle for less, Erik's too careful with money for that. The savings would hold us, but they're house money, and I'd feel sick dipping into them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house would be off, that's the first thing. We'd keep the deposit in the bank as our cushion and stop spending on anything we don't need, no holiday, no new car for Marco. I'd ask round the other hill farms for work, since there are plenty nearby, and I'd stay on at the Lindqvists' as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at night doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I don't get to change anything, I only get to stop. Stop the house, stop spending, stop planning. With ten years you can at least turn round slowly, like a tractor and trailer in a gateway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be most worried about apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf, the part-timer. He's fifty-four and he only does the jobs a robot could do first, the feeding and the fencing. Marco would be all right, I think, because somebody has to fix the machines, at least for a while.

S2.say: I'd say I don't believe it until I see a robot prune an apple tree properly. Privately I'd tell my mum I was scared, but in public I'd keep my head down.
S2.think: If it's real, two years is no time, and this farm is my one skill. The owners wouldn't keep me on if a robot was cheaper, and dipping into our house money would make me feel sick.
S2.do: Calls off the house purchase and keeps the deposit as a cushion. Stops non-essential spending, such as a holiday and a new car, asks around other hill farms for work and stays at her farm as long as she's wanted.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at night doing sums.
S2.quote: With two years I don't get to change anything, I only get to stop.
S2.fieldNote: Her strong savings are emotionally tied to the house, so using them feels like loss even though they'd protect her. She expects her mechanic partner to fare better than she would. She would show fear only to her mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, show me the robot pruning the apples. But I'd probably say it a bit more quietly, because five years is long enough that people would start to see things on farms. I'd listen more than I'd talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to make one change, I think, if I'm honest with myself. I'm not going to learn computers. But there are things like dry-stone walling and hedge-laying, old skills that hill farms still pay for, and I could get good at those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a dry-stone walling course in the first year, the weekend one the farmers' group runs. I'd keep saving, maybe more than now, and buy the smaller house rather than the mill cottage. I'd wait to see what the Lindqvists buy before doing anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an anxious I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why dry-stone walling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because nobody's built a robot that can pick the right stone off a pile by looking at it. Old Mr Lindqvist taught me a bit, and he says I've got the eye for it. It might be the last job left on a hill, fixing the walls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd be slow and not wrong. Is this you being slow, or getting ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. It's getting ahead by going backwards. I'm happy with that.

S3.say: I'd still say show me the robot pruning the apples, but more quietly, because people would start seeing things on farms. I'd listen more than I'd talk.
S3.think: Five years is enough to make one change if I'm honest. I won't learn computers, but old skills like dry-stone walling and hedge-laying are still paid for on hill farms.
S3.do: Takes a weekend dry-stone walling course in the first year and saves more than now. Buys the smaller house instead of the mill cottage and waits to see what the farm owners buy before doing more.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way she can work with.
S3.quote: It's getting ahead by going backwards.
S3.fieldNote: Given more time, she finds a way to adapt that fits her resistance: a traditional craft rather than new tech. The idea comes from the old farmer's praise of her eye for stone. She noticed and accepted the contradiction with her earlier caution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change, so no point panicking. That's what I'd say at the pub, and I'd probably believe it most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven, and that's young enough to try something else if I have to. But I know I won't move until I have to. That's just how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy the house, honestly, but the smaller one. Keep working, maybe do the walling course in a couple of years. I'd wait and see what happens at the dealer, because Marco would hear about the robots before anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there in the background, like a bad knee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Marco is your early warning, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much. When the farmers come into the dealer asking about robots instead of tractors, he'll know. He'd tell me, and I'd still probably say let's see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to name one thing that would make you move sooner, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik buying a robot. If he did, I'd know it was coming for my job, because he only buys what pays for itself. That's when I'd stop saying let's see.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change, so there's no point panicking. That's what I'd say at the pub, and I'd believe it most days.
S4.think: At thirty-seven I'd be young enough to try something else, but I know I won't move until I have to. That's just how I am.
S4.do: Buys the smaller house and keeps working, perhaps taking the walling course in a couple of years. Waits for signs from her partner at the tractor dealer and acts only once the farm's owner buys a robot.
S4.feel: Uneasy, a background worry like a bad knee.
S4.quote: When the farmers come into the dealer asking about robots instead of tractors, he'll know.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she relaxes into her usual approach of waiting, and says plainly that she won't move until forced. Her partner's job at the dealer is her early warning system. She named a clear trigger for action: the owner buying a robot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to stop everything, the house, all of it. What would help is the farms round here being given time, some rule that robots come in slowly, and maybe help for people like Yusuf who are too old to start again. For me, just knowing what's coming early enough.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the apples. Everyone thinks farming is cows and tractors, but the orchard's the bit I'd miss most. Old Mr Lindqvist planted half those trees, and I'd hate a machine to be the one that pulls them out.

headlineQuote: Old Mr Lindqvist planted half those trees, and I'd hate a machine to be the one that pulls them out.
portrait: Bianca Costa, 27, has worked six years on a hill farm with beef cattle, hay meadows and an old apple orchard, and she never uses AI tools. She and her partner Marco, a mechanic at the tractor dealer, have saved a house deposit. She takes the AI Plateau as a green light to buy, trusts steep hills to slow things under Steady Disruption, and is alarmed by AGI by 2028 because she'd have to stop every plan. With five or ten years she picks an old craft, dry-stone walling, as her way forward, while admitting she won't move until she has to.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she would have to stop everything, including buying the house.
whatWouldHelp: Robots being brought into farms slowly by some rule, help for older workers like Yusuf, and knowing what's coming early enough.
